Stairs
STAIRZ
n. pl.
From Anglo-Saxon staeger, from stigan, to climb or ascend. Webster 1828: a series of steps by which persons ascend to a higher room. In Scripture the stairs are where a man stands to be seen and heard, and where a dove hides.

Biblical Definition

Solomon’s temple had a concealed ascent: The door for the middle chamber was in the right side of the house: and they went up with winding stairs into the middle chamber, and out of the middle into the third (1 Kings 6:8). The side chambers rose in three storeys and the stair turned inside the wall, unseen from the court. Nehemiah records the rebuilding of another set: the wall of the pool of Siloah by the king's garden, and unto the stairs that go down from the city of David (Nehemiah 3:15) — ordinary masonry named in a chapter that is a roll of honour for people who repaired what was in front of their own houses. In the New Testament the stairs of the Antonia fortress become a pulpit: when he had given him licence, Paul stood on the stairs, and beckoned with the hand unto the people. And when there was made a great silence, he spake unto them in the Hebrew tongue (Acts 21:40) — a prisoner between a mob and a Roman garrison, preaching in the mob’s own language. And the Song places the beloved in the hidden turn of a stair: O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance (Song of Solomon 2:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines STAIR as a step; one of a series of steps by which persons ascend to a higher room or level; and in the plural, a flight of such steps.

expand to see more

STAIR, n. — A step; a stone or a frame of boards or planks by which a person rises one step.

In the plural, STAIRS, a flight of steps by which persons ascend to a higher room or story.

WINDING STAIRS, a flight of steps turning about a newel or centre.

STAIRCASE, n. — The part of a building which contains the stairs.

Anglo-Saxon staeger, from stigan, to ascend — the root of sty and stile.

Key Scripture

1 Kings 6:8 — "The door for the middle chamber was in the right side of the house: and they went up with winding stairs into the middle chamber, and out of the middle into the third."

Nehemiah 3:15 — "But the gate of the fountain repaired Shallun the son of Colhozeh, the ruler of part of Mizpah; he built it, and covered it, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof, and the wall of the pool of Siloah by the king's garden, and unto the stairs that go down from the city of David."

Acts 21:40 — "And when he had given him licence, Paul stood on the stairs, and beckoned with the hand unto the people. And when there was made a great silence, he spake unto them in the Hebrew tongue, saying,"

Song of Solomon 2:14 — "O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely."

Modern Corruption

Nehemiah 3 is a chapter of names and masonry that modern reading skips, and it contains the plainest biblical picture of ordinary people repairing what lies in front of their own door.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of unremarkable work. Nehemiah 3 lists goldsmiths, apothecaries, merchants and rulers, each repairing a named section — and repeatedly, over against his house. The chapter also records that the nobles of Tekoa put not their necks to the work of their Lord (Nehemiah 3:5), which is the only censure in the list and falls on the men best able to help. Stairs, doors, locks and bars are named individually. A church culture that measures usefulness by visibility has no category for this chapter, and would not have written it down. Scripture keeps the record, which is itself the doctrine: God notices the section of wall in front of a man’s own house.

Acts 21:40 is worth pausing over for what Paul does with a moment of extremity. He has been dragged from the temple, beaten, and rescued by a Roman commander who assumed he was an Egyptian revolutionary. Standing in chains on the fortress stairs, with licence granted to speak, he addresses the crowd in Hebrew and gives them his testimony. He does not defend his liberty, protest his treatment, or address the Romans who held him; he preaches to the people who had just tried to kill him, in their own tongue, and the change of language alone quiets them. That is the apostolic instinct about a platform: it is for the gospel, and the audience is the one that needs it most.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew maalah (H4609), a step or ascent, the word also used of the Songs of Degrees; lul (H3883), a winding stair; Greek anabathmos (G304), a flight of steps.

expand to see more

Hebrew lul (H3883) — a spiral or winding stair; the concealed ascent of Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 6:8).

Hebrew maalah (H4609) — a step, stair, or ascent; also the title-word of the Psalms of Degrees.

Greek anabathmos (G304) — a flight of steps; the stairs of the Antonia fortress (Acts 21:40).

Hebrew madregah (H4095) — a steep place or stair; the secret places of the stairs (Song of Solomon 2:14).

Greek Hebrais dialektos — the Hebrew tongue, the language that quieted the crowd (Acts 21:40).

Usage

"They went up with winding stairs into the middle chamber (1 Kings 6:8) — an ascent turning inside the wall, unseen from the court."

"Unto the stairs that go down from the city of David (Nehemiah 3:15) — masonry named in a roll of honour."

"Paul stood on the stairs, and beckoned with the hand unto the people (Acts 21:40) — a prisoner preaching in the mob’s own language."
